lede: Spark doesn't touch your data when you write `filter` or `select`. It writes down a plan, and only runs it when you ask for an answer. Knowing which lines plan and which lines run explains most of how PySpark behaves.
objectives: Explain why a transformation returns straight away and reads no rows
Bring rows back to Python with `collect`, `first` and `take`, and read values from a row

blocks.md:
The `orders` table above has one row per order in a small shop. In every example on this page it's already loaded as a DataFrame called `orders`, and `F` is `pyspark.sql.functions`.

Everything you do with a DataFrame is one of two kinds of step:

- A **transformation** describes a new DataFrame from an old one: `filter` keeps some rows, `select` keeps some columns, `limit(n)` keeps at most `n` rows. It returns a new DataFrame **straight away** and runs nothing.
- An **action** asks for an answer: `show()`, `count()`, `collect()`, `first()`, `take(n)`. This is the moment Spark actually reads data and does the work.

This lesson uses `filter` and `select` only as examples of transformations. Lessons 9 and 10 cover them properly.

blocks.title: A transformation gives back a plan
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

paid = orders.filter(F.col("status") == "paid")
print(paid)
blocks.note: Printing `paid` shows its columns and their types, but no rows: none have been read yet. `paid` is a new DataFrame that only knows how to get its rows.

blocks.md: A DataFrame is a **plan** until an action runs it. That's called **lazy evaluation**. Spark waits on purpose: once it sees the whole plan, it can skip columns and rows you never use, and do several steps in one pass over the data.

blocks.title: An action runs the plan
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

paid = orders.filter(F.col("status") == "paid")
paid.show()
print(paid.count(), "of", orders.count(), "orders are paid")
blocks.note: `show()` and `count()` are actions, so this time Spark reads the orders. `orders` still has all 12 rows: a transformation makes a new DataFrame and never changes the old one.

blocks.md: Transformations chain: each one adds a step to the plan. Nothing runs until the action at the end, and then all the steps run together.

blocks.title: Chain steps, then act once
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

web = orders.filter(F.col("channel") == "web")
web_totals = web.select("order_id", "total")
first_two = web_totals.limit(2)
first_two.show()
blocks.note: Three transformations build the plan; only `show()` runs it. Which rows `limit` keeps isn't promised unless the rows are sorted (lesson 11). On this small table it keeps the first two in file order.

blocks.md:
`show()` prints rows for you to look at. To use the values in Python, bring rows back with an action:

- `collect()` returns **every** row as a Python list. Fine for a few rows; on a big table it can overwhelm your program.
- `take(n)` returns a list of at most `n` rows.
- `first()` returns just the first row.

Each row is a `Row`. Read a value with `row["column"]`.

blocks.title: Bring rows back to Python
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

web = orders.filter(F.col("channel") == "web").select("order_id", "total")

rows = web.collect()
print(len(rows), "web orders")

first = web.first()
print(first["order_id"], first["total"])

print(web.take(2))
blocks.note: `collect()` brought back all three web orders as a list, `first()` one `Row`, and `take(2)` a list of two. `total` comes back as a Python `Decimal`, which keeps the exact cents.

blocks.md: Lazy doesn't mean careless. When you add a step, Spark checks it against the columns it knows about, without reading any rows. A misspelt column fails on the line where you wrote it, not later at the action.

blocks.title: A wrong column name fails straight away
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

big = orders.filter(F.col("totl") > 200)
print("never printed")
blocks.note: There's no action here at all, yet Spark stops on the `filter` line: it knows `orders` has no `totl` column and suggests the names it does have.

blocks.md: To see the plan itself, call `explain()` on a DataFrame. It's not an action: it prints the plan without running it.

blocks.title: Look at the plan
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

web_totals = orders.filter(F.col("channel") == "web").select("order_id", "total")
web_totals.explain()
blocks.note: Read it from the bottom up: scan the CSV file, keep the web rows (`Filter`), keep two columns (`Project`). The scan's `ReadSchema` lists only the three columns the plan needs: because Spark saw the whole plan first, it skips the rest. The numbers after `#` are Spark's own labels for columns.

concept.prompt: Which of these is an action?
concept.why: `count()` asks for an answer, so Spark runs the plan. `filter`, `select` and `limit` are transformations: each returns a new DataFrame and runs nothing.

concept.prompt: What happens when the line `paid = orders.filter(F.col("status") == "paid")` runs?
choices: Spark reads every order and keeps the paid ones in memory
Spark builds a new DataFrame that describes the paid orders, without reading any rows
The unpaid rows are removed from `orders`
concept.why: A transformation only adds a step to a plan. Rows are read when an action, such as `show()` or `count()`, runs that plan. `orders` itself never changes.

concept.prompt: You write `orders.filter(F.col("totl") > 200)` with a typo and no action after it. What happens?
choices: Nothing, until an action runs the plan
An error on that line, because Spark checks column names as you build the plan
concept.why: Spark checks each step against the columns it knows as soon as you write it, without reading data. The `AnalysisException` points at the `filter` line.

review: Transformations such as `filter`, `select` and `limit` return a new DataFrame straight away and run nothing.
Actions such as `show`, `count`, `collect`, `first` and `take` run the plan and give you an answer.
A DataFrame is a plan until an action runs it. This is lazy evaluation, and it lets Spark skip work you don't need.
A transformation never changes the DataFrame it started from.
`collect()` returns every row as a list, `take(n)` at most `n`, `first()` one `Row`; read values with `row["column"]`.
`explain()` prints the plan without running it. Wrong column names fail as soon as you write the step.
